analysis.one_liner: Offers federal grants to states that license handgun buyers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and got no vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Justice Department give grants to states, cities, and tribes that have laws requiring a license to buy a handgun. To qualify, a state's licensing law must require applicants to be 21 or older, pass a background check, submit fingerprints, and renew the license at least every five years. It does not require any state to adopt licensing — it only pays states that choose to.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that adopt or strengthen handgun licensing, through a program the bill's findings say is linked to lower firearm homicide and suicide rates; local law enforcement agencies that would administer and be funded to run licensing programs.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes competitive Justice Department grants to states, local governments, and Indian tribes to develop, implement, and evaluate handgun purchaser licensing programs.

Conditions eligibility on licensing laws requiring applicants to be at least 21, lawfully present, pass a criminal history check, submit fingerprints and photos, and renew the license every five years or less.
Cites research that adopting a licensing law in Connecticut was associated with a 27.8% drop in firearm homicide rates and a 32.8% drop in firearm suicide rates.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers through appropriations, whose amount the bill leaves open ('such sums as may be necessary'); handgun buyers in participating states would face license applications, fees set by their state, and waiting associated with background checks and fingerprinting.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and handgun buyers in participating states

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes unlimited appropriations without setting a funding level, leaving the program's cost and scope entirely to later appropriations decisions.

The licensing requirements add an application step at a law enforcement agency, with fingerprints, photographs, and renewal at least every five years, which gun-rights opponents argue burdens lawful purchasers, particularly in rural areas far from licensing offices.

The bill's own findings note that most crime guns traced in licensing states come from states without such laws, meaning a voluntary grant program would leave trafficking from non-participating states untouched unless many states joined.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real but indirect: the bill does not mandate licensing anywhere, it only subsidizes states that choose it, and the cited research links such laws to substantial reductions in gun homicides and suicides. The costs are modest and mostly borne voluntarily by participating states' residents. The main design weakness is that a voluntary incentive leaves the problem — gun trafficking from non-licensing states — largely intact if few states opt in, which is what happened: the bill died with minimal support.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Van Hollen introduced the bill with Blumenthal and Murphy as cosponsors on January 26, 2023.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of expanded handgun licensing, and the handgun industry, are better off: the bill died in committee without a vote, so no federal incentives for purchaser licensing were created. States that already license buyers gained nothing, and none were newly nudged into adopting licensing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun-rights opponents and the firearms industry

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create federal grants for state handgun purchaser licensing programs.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only two senators to do so.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no markup, no vote, no report.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, so the partisan split was never tested; all three Senate supporters were Democrats, and no Republican supported it on the record.

industries.note: Handgun purchaser licensing, where states adopt it with these grants, is associated in the bill's own findings with fewer firearm homicides and suicides, which would mean fewer handgun sales in participating states. The bill's voluntary design limits the impact, and the industry had nothing to fear since the bill died without action.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies would receive federal money to run licensing programs they would otherwise fund themselves, in states that choose to license buyers.
